text:
Here's an easy question. How many words are in this sentence? Is can't one word, or two? Does the period after Doctor end the sentence? Is the dollar sign a word? You read it in a second. A computer gets one flat string of sixty-two characters. Nothing in it says where a word starts, where a sentence ends, or what any of it means. Natural language processing, NLP for short, closes that gap. It turns unstructured text into structure a program can compute with. Part of what makes that hard is ambiguity.

Language is full of it, and we resolve it so easily that we rarely notice. One word can mean two things. A bank is the side of a river, or a place for money. That's lexical ambiguity. One sentence can group two ways. I saw the man with the telescope. Did I use it, or was he holding it? That's structural ambiguity. And a word can point two ways. The trophy didn't fit in the case because it was too big. What was too big? You know it's the trophy. A computer has no idea. That's referential ambiguity. Real text is also messy in plainer ways.

Contractions hide words. Don't is do, and not. One period ends a sentence, shortens Doctor, and marks a decimal point. Apple, the company, isn't apple, the fruit. Run, runs, running and ran are four spellings of one idea. And New York is one place, written as two words. Each of these is the reason a later step exists. So why not just split on the spaces?
